#4634. Mercedes-Benz Will Sell a C111 Rotary Supercar Prototype for the First Time in History

No copies of the 1970s-era gullwing wedges have ever been available for public ownership before.

There’s no shortage of rare, collectable, crazy-desirable classic Mercedes-Benz vehicles out there for the discerning car collector. Some of the Three-Pointed Star’s cars have gone down in history among the most expensive automobiles ever sold; there’s the $11.8 million 1936 Mercedes-Benz 540 K Special Roadster by Sindelfingen, the $10.2 million 2002 Mercedes-Benz CLK GTR Roadster, and of course, the 1955 300 SLR Uhlenhaut Coupé that sold for over $140 million back in 2022, making it the world’s most valuable car.

But no matter how rich, how connected, how much of a master of the universe you are, you’ve never been able to buy one of Mercedes-Benz’s most ground-breaking machines: the rotary-powered C111. Or at least, that was the case. Come next year, for the very first time, one lucky person will be able to take the Apollo-era wundercar home.

Fans of the brand certainly need no introduction to this wedge-shaped beauty, but for those of you who might not be as current on your Mercedes history, the C111 was revealed at the 1969 International Motor Show (IAA) in Frankfurt, less than two months after Neil Armstrong plopped his boots on the moon. The idea was to create a gullwinged successor to the iconic W198-gen 300SL that dominated racing in the 1950s, packed with then-impressive technology: Wankel rotary engines, fiberglass bodywork, and multi-link rear suspension, all wrapped in a gorgeous period design.

Yet while 17 prototypes were ultimately made, the car never entered production. Rumor has it that interested parties practically channeled Philip J. Fry shouting “Shut up and take my money” by mailing blank checks to the company’s home office, but Mercedes said no dice, citing the Wankel motor’s inability to play nicely with the 1973 oil crisis. (That also kept the motor from winding up in the S-Class, as Mercedes-Benz Classic head of collection Dennis Heck said.) Instead, the copies served as company test beds for years, performing tasks like high-speed testing at Nardo with a variety of different powertrains and aerodynamic kits.

The car in question that will be up for grabs is the third one ever made, a C111-II variant known internally as “Car 33” that comes equipped with its original 2.4-liter 4-rotor engine making 345 horsepower and 289 lb-ft connected to a 5-speed manual gearbox. It was used as part of the Mercedes test fleet, trialing features like anti-lock brakes and a component to empty its twin fuel tanks at even rates—a handy feature in a car capable of 186 miles per hour.

The car was restored to working order two years ago at the Mercedes-Benz Classic Center, although the patina of the Weißherbst-colored exterior and gray-and-white houndstooth patterned interior was kept delightfully intact. As of last month’s photo shoot, its odometer showed 24,766 kilometers—15,355 miles.

The C111 in question will hit the auction block on February 3, 2027, at the Palais du Louvre as part of RM Sotheby’s Retromobile Paris auctions, with the funds raised by the sale used to help the automaker further develop the Mercedes-Benz museum in Stuttgart, including the creation of a digital twin of the museum that will let people access it virtually.

Given its provenance, I would not expect it to go cheap. Neither does the company. “We do believe it will come to a significant double-digit euro [price at auction],” CEO of Mercedes-Benz Heritage GmbH Marcus Breitschwerdt told Road & Track.

“It’s gonna be in excess of twenty-five [million] euros,” RM Sotheby’s president Gord Duff added. “There will be strong activity. It’s one of those things you could never get until now.”

And if you’re thinking, Ehh, they’ve broken the seal on sales, I’ll wait until they auction off another one—well, you’d better be prepared to hold off until 2051 or so, because Mercedes says this sale includes a contractual commitment that it will not sell any more C111s for the next 25 years. Should you be interested in bidding, you can find out more here.

Will Sabel Courtney is a contributing editor at Road & Track. A 12-year veteran of journalism, he formerly worked at Gear Patrol, The Drive, and RIDES Magazine, and contributed to the New York Daily News and Jalopnik, among other outlets. You can often find him test-driving new cars in New York City, cursing the slow-moving traffic surrounding him.

Published Nov 18, 2026 3:54 PM EST

UPDATE, November 19, 2026, 4:15 p.m. EST: Fiona the hippo has died.

Fiona the hippo remains under the watchful eyes of veterinarians and staff at the Cincinnati Zoo after swallowing a hat last week. As a full-grown hippo, surgery is not an option for Fiona, but her caretakers remain hopeful she will pass the foreign object naturally.

Last week, a knit hat entered her enclosure at the Cincinnati Zoo and the almost 10-year-old hippo ate it. Given her size, zookeepers initially thought she’d simply pass the hat, but it remains stuck in her digestive track. She has undergone a colonoscopy using a 9-foot scope and multiple ultrasounds that show intestinal bunching, indicating her body is continuing to try and expel the hat. Caretakers have continued to give her fluids and sedate her when necessary for tests.

“Fiona ingested an object that a visitor accidentally tossed into her habitat,” the Cincinnati Zoo said in a statement. “Our veterinary team and hippo care staff are monitoring her around the clock and doing everything they can to help her pass the object safely. Her care team is cautiously optimistic that she will pass it and return to her usual self. Fiona will remain off habitat until this is resolved. We will share updates as we have more information.”

The zoo also reminded patrons to be careful with their things when observing animals: “Please help us keep our animals safe by securing your belongings and taking extra care near habitats. Ingesting foreign objects can cause serious health problems for animals. If something falls into a habitat, please notify a Zoo staff member immediately.”

On Wednesday, November 18, the zoo shared a new approach in Fiona’s ongoing treatment: a vibration plate borrowed from a local Ohio horse farm. Fiona could be seen standing on the plate, vocalizing to caretakers. “The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass,” the team explained.

Fiona first captured the internet’s heart in 2017, when she was born six weeks premature. Baby hippos typically weigh about 100 pounds at birth, but tiny Fiona tipped the scales at a mere 29 pounds. She was the smallest known hippo to survive such a low birth weight. As she grew, Fiona took social media and the real world by storm: she photobombed an engagement shoot, had a local ice cream named in her honor, and even starred in her own reality-TV series appropriately called “The Fiona Show.”  Her surprise baby brother Fritz was born in 2022, after their mother’s birth control went “on the fritz.”

#4632. ‘Ferritin Face’: What Low Iron Actually Does (and Doesn't Do) to Your Appearance

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Social media influencers claim that having a “ferritin face” may indicate you’re low in iron.

Ferritin is a protein that helps your body store iron. You need iron in order to make healthy red blood cells, which carry oxygen from your lungs to the rest of your body. Iron is also important for bone marrow, organs, healthy muscles, and brain development.

As “ferritin face” makes its way across social media platforms, users are describing several tell-tale signs, including:

Users have also shared images of their face before and after taking iron supplements or getting an iron infusion. Videos about “ferritin face” have garnered millions of views on various platforms.

However, medical professionals state that your appearance alone is not enough to diagnose iron deficiency.

“It’s important to understand that ferritin face is not a medical diagnosis, nor is it a confirmed symptom of iron deficiency. While some people with iron deficiency can appear pale due to low hemoglobin levels in their red blood cells, there are many other symptoms to consider,” said Daniel Atkinson, a general practitioner in the United Kingdom and clinical lead at Treated.

“Notably, these symptoms are also present in many different conditions, and their presence does not necessarily mean iron deficiency anemia or even low ferritin levels. Similar features are seen in people with iron processing and absorption issues, such as gluten intolerance, or in urgent sudden blood loss scenarios,” added Jonathan Jennings, MD, board certified internist at Medical Offices of Manhattan.

Iron deficiency can affect your skin and appearance. These signs are often subtle, but may include:

In some ways, the social media videos are correct. Your skin and face can change when your iron levels are low.

“The facial signs people point to, like pale skin and a washed-out look, mostly come from anaemia, when your haemoglobin has dropped. But iron deficiency and anaemia aren’t the same thing,” said Thom Phillips, a general practitioner in the United Kingdom and Chief Medical Officer at Forth. “By the time low iron shows on your face, your stores are usually close to empty.”

It is important to speak with a healthcare professional, who will run blood tests such as a complete blood count and ferritin levels.

It is also important not to take iron supplements without first checking with your healthcare professional, because having too much iron in your body can also cause negative effects.

Too little and too much iron could raise your risk of infection, which is why it’s important not to take supplements without medical supervision.

The signs and symptoms of iron deficiency can depend on whether you are anemic or not. Some of the early signs may include:

“These symptoms typically occur because your body produces fewer red blood cells, which results in less oxygen being delivered throughout your body, making you feel tired and weak,” said Atkinson.

While your facial appearance can be a sign that something isn’t right, healthcare professionals consider other symptoms and how you feel overall.

They also rely on blood tests to confirm the diagnosis and guide treatment.

“The misinformation is the idea that you can spot it yourself. That leads to two problems: people with low iron who look fine assume they’re OK, and people who look tired start taking iron supplements they don’t need,” said Phillips.

Atkinson also noted that factors such as different settings and environmental conditions can affect how your face appears.

That being said, the “ferritin face” trend may help bring awareness to certain symptoms and when to get them checked.

“[This] trend may raise some awareness about iron deficiency anemia and how low iron levels can impact daily life,” said Atkinson.

“Fatigue and lightheadedness are common side effects of low iron, but it manifests in other ways too, such as paler skin or increased hair shedding, which can be concerning for many people. If you experience these symptoms, you should let your doctor know so they can help treat the condition appropriately,” he said.

#4631. Mowing milestone: Greenzie surpasses 255,000 autonomous miles mowed

Autonomous lawncare specialists Greenzie passed a major milestone with their self-driving mowers last week, surpassing 255,000 cumulative robomowing miles. For context, that’s far enough to mow every inch of space between the Earth and Moon.

Greenzie announced the self-driving milestone last week, and it’s genuinely impressive, reflecting Greenzie Powered Autonomy mowing more than 9 billion (with a b) square feet of turf across more than 200 commercial customers, 45 US states, and more than 500,000 equivalent man-hours of mowing.

And, while I might have pointed the fact that Greenzie mowers have covered more miles in its press release than Daimler’s entire hydrogen truck fleet, the company really seems to be leaning into the Moon angle.

“We mowed to the moon, but the real achievement is the commercial experience behind those miles,” says Charles Brian Quinn, co-founder and CEO of Greenzie and almost definitely the guy who first came up with the lunar lawncare line. “Every mile represents equipment working on real properties with commercial crews. That experience has shaped our technology, strengthened our OEM partnerships and taught us how to help customers successfully integrate autonomy into their daily operations.”

Greenzie develops autonomous packages for, and maintains OEM relationships with electric brands Mean Green Electric Mowers (whose Vanquish Autonomous commercial mower is shown, above), and Greenworks Commercial, as well as gas-powered brands like Bobcat and Wright Manufacturing. Regardless of what powers the mowers, Greenzie supplies the self-driving technology and integration expertise, while its OEM partners develop and manufacture the equipment that does the actual cutting, clearing, and whatever else their clients need.

“Successful autonomy requires more than capable technology,” said Steve Bush, chief operating officer of Greenzie. “Customers need to understand where autonomy fits into their operations, how to prepare their crews and how to measure success. We have spent years learning those lessons alongside our customers and OEM partners, creating a more consistent path to adoption as the industry grows.”

The Mean Green Vanquish Autonomous featured gere is a fully electric, stand-on, zero-turn (ZTR) mower built around an all-day-ready 22 kWh li-ion battery pack and featuring a 60″ rear-discharge mulching deck.

Mean Green claims that the combination of big battery and the electric motors that drive the ZTR mower and spin up its blades are good up to eight hours of continuous mowing on a charge, with an aluminum chassis and deck helping to keep the machine’s overall weight down for easier towing maximum efficiency.

The company says the mower can operate in either manual or autonomous mode, with Greenzie’s self-driving software supported by six depth-sensing stereo cameras providing 360-degree vision, RTK-corrected GPS, and visual-inertial odometry for onboard site mapping and precise positioning, which Greenzie says allows the mower to detect obstacles up to twenty feet away, recognize designated keep-out zones, and automatically return to its starting point when called back.

A top speed of 11.5 mph and the ability to repeat saved mowing routes, the Vanquish is designed to give commercial landscaping crews another productive worker without adding another person to the payroll … which, with a $60,000 asking price, is money they will probably still need.

Let’s get some pro-labor rage going in the comments, and don’t forget to mention what kind of paycheck you’d need to get to go work in landscaping 2,000+ hours a year while you’re there.

#4630. BMW Is Recalling i5 and i7 EVs Over Software Error That Could Lead to an Electric Shock

The automaker is recalling 286 examples of the electric sedans after discovering some received the wrong high-voltage battery software.

A classic BMW 2002 is a simple, mechanical machine. However, a modern BMW sedan is a rolling computer, one that relies heavily on software. And when that software is buggy, issues can arise—which is why the software is tested extensively before going to production. But what happens when that test software mistakenly makes it into production cars?

According to a National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) recall report, BMW is recalling 286 i5 and i7 electric sedans in the United States because some vehicles may have been equipped with testing software, instead of the production software intended to manage high-voltage battery charging. In rare cases, this could expose people to a higher risk of an electric shock.

The recall includes 236 examples of the 2026–2027 BMW i5, including the eDrive40, xDrive40, and M60 variants. Another 50 vehicles are 2027 BMW i7 50 xDrive and 60 xDrive models. All the affected vehicles were manufactured between May and July 2026.

BMW first became aware of the issue on October 8, 2026, when high-voltage battery charging port supplier TE Connectivity Solutions GmbH alerted the automaker. An investigation ensued, and it was discovered that some charging units were mistakenly shipped with test software instead of production software. BMW is not aware of any injuries or accidents related to this problem.

No hardware changes are required to rectify the issue, and the affected vehicles will require a software update. The recall report does not specify that this can be fixed via an over-the-air update, so a trip to the dealer will likely be required.

BMW plans to mail owner notification letters beginning December 25, 2026, although we doubt the U.S.P.S. will be doing much picking up or delivery that day. Starting that same date, owners can also check their vehicle's recall status through the NHTSA recall website by using their VIN, but we suggest waiting until after the kids are done opening presents.

#4629. Audiophiles are eating good this December with new headphones and earbuds from classic American brands

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 4:30 PM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn more ›

If you’re into personal audio, you might not want to spend all your money during Black Friday/Cyber Monday (but feel free to spend a little, and keep coming back here for some great suggestions as to how). Just within the last week, several innovative new headphones and earbuds have been announced, so read on for wired, wireless, and TWS options for every taste.

First up is Klipsch, the Hope, Arkansas-based heritage brand celebrating its 80th anniversary. But that doesn’t mean the acoustic design team is stuck in the past. Originally teased as Atlas at CES 2026 during a behind-closed-doors preview alongside powered standmount speakers and other surprises, the new Stratos Series uses an atypical (for headphones) two-way coaxial array, which aligns a mid/bass driver with a dynamic tweeter on a single axis to deliver low-distortion, high-efficiency, full-range sound.

The 380g Klipsch HP-2 (above) is the closed-back option, with a 40mm bio-cellulose woofer and 10mm tweeter achieving a frequency response of 15 Hz-18 kHz (+/-5 dB), plus isolation for more critical monitoring. The 458g HP-3 (below, and the one we’re most excited to audition) is a semi-open-back design that expands the woofer to 50mm to make up for some of the low end typically traded for a more expansive soundstage, and it achieves 16 Hz-22 kHz (+/-5 dB). Both promise “warm, punchy bass and crisp, sparkly highs,” and the pre-production units I heard in January delivered a good bright/bouncy balance, with rich, fun-colored but still composed mids as I recall (though it’s been many months removed).

Both models have an appropriately mid-century modern aesthetic, with auburn-stained sapele wood earcups and copper accents, machined aluminum yokes and contact points, Klipsch Heritage Twitchell grille cloth, replaceable microseude earpads, and protein-leather-wrapped open-cell-foam-filled headbands. Both 4.4mm balanced and 3.5mm unbalanced cables (plus a 1/4-inch adapter) with dual-mono connectors are included.

While both the Stratos HP-2 and HP-3 can be paired with smartphones and dongles of all sorts, they’ll really open up with a more refined signal chain, like the simultaneously announced $649.99 Onkyo HA-70, featuring two premium ESS ES9039Q2M SABRE DACs feeding an amplifier with plentiful inputs and three gain settings versatile enough to drive sensitive IEMs to 600Ω flagship headphones.

Compared to Klipsch, Brooklyn’s Grado Labs is a relatively young’un at the spry age of 73. First (and still) known for decades of producing phono cartridges, the family-owned company expanded into distinctive, hand-built headphones in the late ’80s (and still produces some fabulous flagships). The GW200 carries that tradition into something you can carry. The 235g GW200 takes a 44m S paper-composite diaphragm derived from the drivers in the company’s multi-thousand-dollar Signature line and puts it in an open-back wireless headphone. This helps deliver expressive bass and treble articulation within a frequency response of 16Hz – 34kHz.

Being open-back means a more spacious presentation with more instrument separation than your typical Bluetooth headphone (at the expense of isolation, of course, so don’t expect these to stand in for ANC travel headphones). Helping ensure this is Bluetooth 5.4 with support for Qualcomm aptX Lossless, aptX Adaptive, aptX HD, aptX, AAC, and SBC, plus 60+ hours of battery life. And there’s a single-sided 3.5mm audio input for passive use in case the battery does run out (or you just prefer an external DAC/amp combo).

As for comfort and tuning, the GW200 comes with the Grado Labs F Cushions but is compatible with Grado’s complete line, so you can change both the physical and sonic feel by swapping them. Another trickle-down from the Signature series is the padded leather headband, which goes nicely with the matte black finish. We’re looking forward to getting a pair to try out.

Over in eastern Texas, Noble Audio has been producing artisan IEMs since the early 2010s (and founder John Moulton was doing custom in-ear monitors for enthusiasts even before that). In recent years, the company has been showing what’s possible when the multiple-driver mentality of IEMs (some costing many thousands of dollars) is turned to portable audio, and the Astrid is the latest example. A tribrid architecture featuring an 8.3mm dynamic driver with a PU diaphragm and an aluminum-magnesium alloy dome, a 6mm planar driver, and one balanced armature in each earpiece, the Astrid brings a wired configuration and sophistication to true wireless earbuds.

The overall tonality of the Astrid is rich, full-bodied, but not boomy … punch but not paunch. While sitting beneath the company’s top TWS model, the 4-driver Prestige Encore, Astrid still delivers a detailed soundstage. What really brings the best out of it is the Audiodo Personal Sound feature, which uses a short tone recognition test to test each ear and saves per-channel adjustments on the earbuds to make up for any anatomically incurred frequency range deficiencies. Then Audiodo Equalizer lets you address sensitivities/preferences, overlaying further adjustments on your personalized curve (3-band on iOS, 5-band on Android). There’s also an assessment-independent 10-band EQ if that level of control is more your vibe.

To ensure the most cohesive playback possible, there’s multipoint Bluetooth 6.0 with high-resolution LDAC/aptX Adaptive support for compatible devices, as well as AAC and SBC. Plus active noise cancellation. Battery life is rated up to 11 hours on a single charge, with the wireless/USB-C case bringing the total carry capacity to 40 hours. All that is wrapped in IPX4 ABS enclosures featuring “divinely beautiful” glass fiber faceplates adorned with a dense lattice of silver filigree, like electro-acoustic etching … a metallic polyphony of colliding chords and intersecting transients.

#4628. Is Tesla rushing out a half-baked Cybercab just to shave MKBHD’s head?

Elon Musk called YouTuber Marques Brownlee “a chicken” early Saturday, hours after Tesla opened invite-only Cybercab orders at $29,990 and Brownlee argued that his famous head-shaving bet isn’t lost.

Tesla has about seven weeks to get a Cybercab into a customer’s hands for under $30,000 before 2027, but the half-baked version of Cybercab that they opened orders for with delivery in December makes it look like it’s just to win this dumb bet.

Surely Tesla isn’t down enough to deliver a half-baked product just to “prove” a YouTuber wrong? Or is it?

After Tesla’s “We, Robot” event in October 2024, Brownlee (MKBHD) said there was no way Tesla would deliver a Cybercab to a customer for $30,000 or less before 2027. If it did, he’d shave his head on camera.

Musk has taken it personally ever since. When the first Cybercab came off the Giga Texas line in February, he replied “Gonna happen 😂” to a bald-MKBHD meme, which we covered at the time. In September, after Brownlee doubled down in a new video, Musk wrote: “I guess he really wants to shave his head 🤷‍♂️”

On Friday, Tesla started inviting “select customers” to buy a Cybercab for personal use. The order page lists $29,990, a mandatory $299 per month Autonomy Subscription, a $1,000 non-refundable deposit, and an estimated delivery of December 2026, only in Tesla’s Texas Robotaxi cities.

As we reported Friday, the car only operates inside Tesla’s Robotaxi geofences. And Tesla’s Cybercab Autonomy Subscription Agreement says it “will not operate” without the $299 plan, bans owners from putting it on the Robotaxi network or using it for ride-hailing, and lets Tesla shrink the operating area at any time.

So Tesla designed a robotaxi, then offered it to select private owners who aren’t allowed to use it as a taxi. Over five years, that’s $47,631 before insurance, registration, and charging. And you are limited to small geofenced areas. If you stop paying Tesla’s monthly fee, which it can change at all times, your cybercab becomes a paperweight.

Brownlee laid out his case Friday night. There are no deliveries yet, the car is invite-only rather than publicly available, and it can’t be used as a cab outside of the existing geofences. He called it “a paperweight if I take this thing home,” though he admits that last point isn’t technically part of the bet.

The memes are everywhere, so let’s go back over the bet: Cybercab publicly available for under $30k by the end of 2026My hair is safe for several reasons1: No deliveries yet. But they’re estimating starting in December so that’s neat2: Invite only, not actually publicly… https://t.co/NCD2aFbe2c

Tesla fans fired back with clips from his September video, where he described a car that “will not ship to regular people like you and me for $30k before the end of 2026.” Whole Mars Catalog, an Elon Musk propagandist whose real name is Omar Qazi, told him to “be a man and honor your word.” Musk reposted it, then replied:

Musk also reposted a Grok answer claiming the current offer “matches” the conditions of the bet.

But around the same time, Musk replied directly to Brownlee’s post about the order page, and it didn’t help Tesla’s case:

“It will be available nationwide, as we receive regulatory approval. But the monthly fee is too high. Should match the cost of Tesla FSD and connectivity for other models, which is more like ~$115/month.”

That’s Tesla’s CEO confirming, a day after launch, that the car can’t be sold outside the areas where it already operates and that its price is wrong. A price that Musk fully controls.

Yes, it looks like Tesla is rushing this out just to win a bet against a Youtuber. Absolutely insane behavior. We’ve seen this movie before. In June 2025, Tesla did a single “autonomous delivery” of a Model Y to meet a Musk deadline, then never did it again.

Tesla always pitched the Cybercab as a vehicle for its Robotaxi network. Now, seven weeks before the deadline, a personal-use version shows up that’s invite-only, Texas-only, banned from doing the one thing it was designed for, and attached to a subscription Musk himself says is too expensive. If you set out to build a product whose main job was letting Musk claim he won a Twitter bet, it would look a lot like this.

This Cybercab offering is completely broken. The value proposition is awful. As others have put it, it’s a permanent variable rate lease starting at $300 a month with a ridiculous $30,000 down payment.

Besides, the bet was "under 30k." Starting price is under 30k, but a subscription is required, which takes it over 30k, just to use it for one day. They could have given the car away for free, and just charged a fee to use it. Doesn't change the total cost.

What do you get for this deal? A 2-seater vehicle that only works in small, incomplete, geo-fenced areas and has no steering wheel to do anything else with it. Meanwhile, Tesla insists that the Model Y, like the ones used in its current Robotaxi service alongside the Cybercab, uses the same self-driving technology.

You can buy one for $40,000, and you get a lot more car than the Cybercab; then you can pay $99 a month for FSD instead of $300 a month. Tesla is supposed to let current Tesla owners drive without supervision in the geo-fenced areas, which would basically be the same product as what Tesla is offering right now with the Cybertruck, but you are not a slave to Tesla, which can brick your car at any time or change the terms.

This offer simply makes no sense, and Musk is sort of admitting it by saying the price should be the same as FSD, not $300 a month.

#4627. Mammograms May Offer Early Insight Into Cardiovascular Disease

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Mammograms are widely used to help detect breast cancer, but they may also offer insight into heart health.

The routine X-ray screening may identify breast arterial calcification (BAC), which is the presence of calcium deposits within the walls of the small arteries in the breast.

On a mammogram, BAC is commonly identified as thin, white, parallel lines that give a “tram-track” appearance.

While BAC is harmless to the breasts, it is associated with a significantly higher risk of cardiovascular disease. A 2022 study found women with BAC were 51% more likely to develop heart disease or experience a stroke than those without it.

Laxmi Mehta, MD, a cardiologist at The Ohio State University Wexner Medical Center, said BAC is associated with cardiovascular risk factors, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol. Additionally, BAC has been connected to:

“The reasons for BAC resulting in higher risks for cardiovascular disease are not definitely determined; however, there are some potential mechanisms, one being that they share similar risk factors that result in vascular injury or metabolic stress that result in vascular calcification and atherosclerosis,” Mehta told Healthline.

Cheng-Han Chen, MD, interventional cardiologist and medical director of the Structural Heart Program at MemorialCare Saddleback Medical Center, added that because BAC and heart disease share many of the same risk factors, “calcium in breast arteries therefore suggests disease in the heart (coronary) and brain arteries as well,” he told Healthline.

While 1 in 39 females in the United States dies from breast cancer each year, cardiovascular disease causes one out of every three deaths, resulting in 1 death per minute.

“Cardiovascular disease is still the most common cause of death in premenopausal women,” Richard Reitherman, MD, PhD, a radiologist and medical director of breast imaging at MemorialCare Breast Center at Orange Coast Medical Center, told Healthline.

“The presentation of cardiovascular disease in premenopausal women is notoriously different than in postmenopausal women, primarily [because] there are no typical symptoms such as chest pain.”

Reitherman said that a prevalent and common health screening procedure such as a mammogram can lead to the early identification of women with silent cardiovascular disease.

“Cardiovascular outcome studies that have included breast arterial calcifications as a risk factor are increasingly reported in the medical literature,” he said.

“The hope is that identifying younger women with silent cardiovascular risks [like BAC along with] appropriate integrated risk identification, analysis, and interventions can significantly reduce mortality in this age group.”

Mehta said there are several reasons BAC has been overlooked as a risk factor for heart disease.

“Mammograms are completed for assessment of breast cancer, and BAC has been historically an ‘incidental’ finding, which is not clinically relevant from an oncologic standpoint,” she said.

Additionally, there is no standardization on quantification of BAC severity, nor is it a required component of mammogram reports, said Mehta.

However, routine reporting of BAC on mammograms is an urgent goal of the American College of Radiology, Society of Breast Imaging, and Medicare, said Reitherman.

In fact, it is gaining traction in the United States. A new Maryland law, passed on October 1, requires mammography centers to notify women when a BAC is detected on their mammogram.

“Automated identification and reporting of these calcifications detected on screening mammograms will become increasingly prevalent in the coming months [and] years,” said Reitherman.

The next step is to identify this group of women to primary care physicians so that appropriate risk evaluation can take place, Reitherman added.

In addition to doctors routinely screening for conditions related to heart disease, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, and high cholesterol, he hopes BAC will also be routinely considered.

“Under current development are protocols to identify patients needing a cardiologist’s training and expertise to appropriately stratify this group of patients,” said Reitherman.

“The common healthcare behavior [of] having regular mammograms not only reduces risk of morbidity and mortality from breast cancer but will hopefully contribute to the reduction of morbidity and mortality from cardiovascular disease in younger women.”

He said this type of integrated healthcare approach demonstrates cross-specialty integration and coordination among women, radiologists, and their healthcare providers to improve women’s lives.

“This is an amazing game-changing opportunity,” Reitherman said.

Mehta said it’s reasonable for women to ask if BAC is present on their mammogram report.

“But if it is not uniformly reported by the radiologist, the individual clinician may not have the answer,” she said.

More research is needed before BAC on mammograms can be used routinely to predict heart disease.

Finding out your BAC could provide additional information to help you and your doctors decide how aggressively to address your cardiovascular risk factors, Chen said.

Reitherman agreed. “The goal of reducing morbidity and mortality from any cause such as cardiovascular disease is based on recognition of risk factors, followed by appropriate lifestyle and pharmacologic interventions,” he said.

#4626. Rare rhino birth caught on camera at England’s Chester Zoo

🛍️ 200+ Black Friday deals actually worth buying 🛍️

Published Nov 18, 2026 7:01 PM EST

On the evening of October 11, a rare greater one-horned rhinoceros (Rhinoceros unicornis) was born at the Chester Zoo in England. Even more exciting, CCTV cameras captured the poignant moment for this threatened species. The footage shows rhino mom Asha giving birth, and the calf’s first unsure steps into the world.

The sex and weight have not been announced yet, and the calf also does not have a name.

At birth, greater one-horned rhino calves weigh about 100 pounds. By comparison, the largest adult greater one-horned rhinos weigh over two tons, or as much as a car.

The team used a combination of experience and non-invasive testing to help plan out the pregnancy. They closely monitored Asha’s behavior and regularly collected samples of her poop. By testing hormone levels in the samples, they could track Asha’s reproductive cycle and identify when she would be most open to mating. This helped the team safely introduce her to Beni the rhino, while a separate analysis helped confirm the pregnancy.

“Asha was pregnant for about 15 months, so it’s a long wait! We had our fingers crossed when she showed signs of labour and we knew we were likely to welcome the calf very soon,” Emma Evison, Team Manager for rhinos said in an e-mailed statement. “It was a big moment for us—and for the conservation breeding programme—when the calf arrived. Any birth can be risky, even for an experienced mum, but fortunately everything went smoothly. The calf was up and about within an hour and feeding shortly afterwards. Asha knows exactly what she’s doing.”

Both mother and calf are reportedly in good health. They remained inside for the first few days following the birth to stay warm, but are now venturing to a special behind-the-scenes paddock outside of the enclosure. The calf is Asha’s fourth with father Beni. Sadly, Beni died in September following a sudden and brief illness.

“Beni was a lovely rhino. He was calm and approachable, helped train animal care specialists and even took part in animal behaviour studies,” added Tom Garland, Assistant Manager of the rhino team at Chester Zoo. “It’s lovely to know that his legacy lives on through this calf.”

While not the largest rhino species in the world, greater one-horned rhinos stand about six feet tall at the shoulder and are the biggest in Asia. They have the smallest horns of any rhino, but also have the biggest teeth. The males will sometimes use these chompers to bite each other while sparring. Currently, about 4,000 greater one-horned rhinos are alive today. They live in India and Nepal, in forests, wetlands, and grasslands. In the early 1990s, trophy hunting and habitat loss almost drove them to extinction.. Poaching for their prized horns also threatened their survival.

While the IUCN Red List of Endangered Species currently lists them as Vulnerable, they remain  at risk of extinction. Many of the rhinos are concentrated into a relatively small number of protected areas, putting their genetic diversity at risk. A lack of genetic diversity can lead to inbreeding and worse health outcomes in general. This new calf is part of a Europe-wide conservation breeding program to help maintain a healthy and genetically diverse population of greater one-horned rhinos living in human care.

“Supporting Asha’s pregnancy has been really exciting,” added conservation scientist John O’Hanlan. “She’s one of relatively few greater one-horned rhinos in Europe actively breeding, so every successful birth is important in maintaining a healthy and genetically diverse population.”

#4625. Waymo Has Been Banned From Operating Autonomous Vehicles on California Freeways, DMV Says

The state has put a halt on the self-driving ride-share company’s high-speed operations due to an “imminent hazard to public safety.”

The California Department of Motor Vehicles has temporarily banned autonomous rideshare operator Waymo from operating on freeways in the Golden State.

The ban went into effect on November 11, and was prompted by an “imminent hazard to public safety,” according to the California DMV. The automotive regulator said two specific incidents in which Waymo vehicles disregarded construction zones and law enforcement, pushed the ban forward, CNN reports.

The California DMV said Waymo will remain banned until it “demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions.” Specifically, the Alphabet-funded autonomous vehicle operator will have to prove that its vehicles can safely detect and respond to construction zones and emergency vehicles.

The freeway restriction applies to revenue ride-share operations, as well as test vehicles. Waymo will continue to operate normally on surface streets in its California markets. Currently, Waymo operates in Los Angeles, San Diego, and the Bay Area.

“Safety is at the foundation of everything we do. Following recent freeway construction zone encounters on U.S. 101 in California that did not involve any injuries or collisions, the California DMV has implemented an operating restriction on freeway operations in the state,” Waymo said in a statement to Road & Track. “In alignment with our safety-first principles, we have also temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets to evaluate our performance. Our ride-hailing service continues to operate safely on surface streets, serving over half a million trips each week. We are working with the California DMV and other state officials diligently and responsibly to resume freeway operations.”

One of the incidents that allegedly spurred this ban was caught on video earlier this month. The video shows California Highway Patrol patrol cars creating a traffic break on Interstate 280 near San Francisco while a Waymo vehicle attempts to pass through the rolling roadblock. California Highway Patrol officers quickly cut in front of the Waymo, which appears to stop the Waymo from attempting to pass again.

This is not the first time Waymo has faced scrutiny related to its highway operations. The company filed a recall with the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration earlier this year over driving software that repeatedly entered freeway construction zones. Waymo also briefly paused highway operations in San Francisco and Los Angeles this May over similar construction zone issues, according to CNN.

The ID. Cross is the all-electric equivalent of the T-Cross, Volkswagen’s smallest and most affordable SUV in Europe and the UK.

The electric SUV is 4,153 mm long, about the same length as the T-Cross, but its dedicated MEB+ platform offers more interior space. It seats five and offers a 475-liter boot, 20 liters more than the gas-powered T-Cross with the rear seats pushed all the way forward.

When the rear seats are folded, the electric ID. Cross offers up to 1,345 liters of overall luggage volume.

Like in Europe, the Volkswagen ID. Cross will be available with two battery packs in the UK: a 37 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) pack and a 52 kWh nickel-manganese-cobalt (NMC) pack.

The ID. Cross with the larger 52 kWh battery offers up to 265 miles of WLTP range, while the 37 kWh version provides up to 194 miles of WLTP range.

The base ID. Cross Life and Style trims with the 37 kWh battery will go on sale in January 2027, with prices starting at £26,985 ($35,500) and £30,400 ($40,100).

Volkswagen said the 52 kWh version is eligible for the UK government’s £1,500 ($2,000) electric car grant. Eligibility for the 37 kWh versions is expected to be confirmed soon.

In Europe, Volkswagen opened orders for the entry-level ID. Cross Trend last month, starting at €27,995 ($31,000) in Germany, including VAT.

As the electric counterpart to its popular T-Cross, Volkswagen brand CEO Thomas Schäfer said the ID. Cross is “modern, reliable, and above all, affordable.”

Sadly, VW has no plans to bring the ID. Cross to the US. In early 2027, it will launch the new ID. Tiguan, which will replace the outgoing ID.4 SUV.

#4622. Ford’s Maverick SV300T Performance Package Brings 300 Horsepower, Courtesy of the Mustang’s Turbocharger

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

But if you want it factory-fresh, be prepared to pay around $50,000.

Ford may be talking up the new Fathom EV as its latest “Model T moment,” but the Blue Oval arguably already had one this century, and it’s called the Maverick. The compact unibody pickup landed in 2021 with a splash worthy of Homer Simpson off a high dive, thanks to its mix of truck bed utility, car-like ride and handling, and available hybrid power, all—technically if not practically—available for under $20,000.

Prices have admittedly climbed since then, even outpacing inflation, and the lineup has seen its fair share of rejiggering over the last five years; the standard engine switched from the hybrid setup to the turbocharged inline-four and then back to the hybrid, for example. The biggest change, however, has been the addition of more fun variants: the off-road focused Tremor and the on-road oriented Lobo, the latter of which aims to Ouija-board the spirit of the original F-150 Lightning to the best of its front-wheel drive-based capabilities.

But what if you already have a Maverick and want to add some zip? Or the Lobo’s just isn’t potent enough for you? Well, that’s where the new Maverick SV300T Package comes into play. But you’ll have to pony up Mustang-like money if you want to see your new compact pickup come equipped with it when you pick up your zero-mile new rig at the local Blue Oval dealer.

The package—which, regrettably, shoves the numerical portion of its name between the letters to keep it from being a proper SVT—comes from the Ford Custom Garage, Dearborn’s in-house upgrade division, and ties together official Ford Racing parts and other Ford accessories to make a sportier Maverick. It’s made for AWD XLT, Lariat, and Lobo models, with the marquee attracting an engine reflash and a Mustang EcoBoost-sourced turbo and an upgraded intercooler to push power from 250 hp and 280 lb-ft to 300 hp and 250 lb-ft; there’s also a Borla exhaust. XLT and Lariat rigs gain Maverick Lobo shocks, lowering springs, and upgraded stabilizer components; they can also opt for an available front brake upgrade. (When we tested it earlier this year on a short autocross course, we found the effects of both power and exhaust both quite noticeable, while the upgraded suspension amped up the delights in the turns.)

On top of that, Ford throws in a few visual upgrades to help make the SV300T’s presence known even before people hear that Borla exhaust. 20-inch wheels come in either black or bronze, as do matching hood and body graphics. Specific lettering on the tailgate also comes along for the ride, and XLT and Lariat trim versions pick up a new lower front spoiler. Plus, if you buy the package with a new Maverick, performance-oriented tires are included, whereas customers adding it after purchase will have to pick them out separately.

Choosing to get the SV300T at purchase, however, means adding $13,395 to the price of a new Lobo, and $15,595 to an XLT or Lariat. Granted, that includes installation and allows owners to wrap it into the truck’s financing, but that still pushes the price to $49,680 for the XLT and $48,090 for the Lobo, based on 2027 model year pricing. (Ford’s announcement says it’s meant for 2025 and 2026 model year trucks, but considering it also mentions that the package is available on new Mavericks, it seems highly unlikely that it would not be available for 2027 ones too.)

Buy SV300T à la carte instead, and the pricing seems a bit more stomach-able; the XLT kit will run you $6075, and the Lobo version $4500. Keep in mind, though, doing so means you’ll have to have an ASE-certified tech handle the install, and you’ll still need to go out and buy new rubber on top of that to make the most of it.

#4621. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD hit an overturned truck at 71 mph, killing 3

A Tesla Model 3 drove into an overturned box truck on I-75 near Naples, Florida, killing two of its passengers and a man who had stopped to help. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, at 71 mph.

Police and local media covered the May 31 crash as a truck wreck in the dark, and none of it mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data, and it lands as Tesla’s monthly crash count hits another record.

Just before 4 a.m. on Sunday, May 31, 2026, the 31-year-old driver of a 2014 Freightliner lost the road near the Pine Ridge Road exit in Collier County, steered back onto southbound I-75, and flipped it, according to the Florida Highway Patrol. The overturned truck ended up blocking the center and outside lanes.

Jonathan Garcia Arias, a 25-year-old Naples man and former Marine, was driving by in a BMW. He pulled over and got out to help the truck driver.

Then a southbound 2023 Tesla with five young men from Naples inside came up on the scene. FHP’s report says the front of the Tesla hit the underside of the overturned truck and Garcia Arias. Two of the Tesla’s passengers, aged 18 and 19, died at the scene, and Garcia Arias died later in the hospital. The 20-year-old driver and two more passengers were seriously hurt.

A few days later, FHP used the crash as a warning about stopping near wrecks on the interstate. Senior Trooper Kenn Watson said the Tesla driver would have seen only the truck’s underside, with “no lights, no reflectors, nothing warning them.”

So that’s the official story. A dark obstacle, a driver who couldn’t see it in time. Nobody said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone was killed or hurt. Tesla filed one for this crash.

It identifies the car as a 2023 Model 3 on a highway, flags a traffic incident on the roadway, and marks the automation “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That means Tesla confirmed through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 71 mph and a fatality, lists the Florida Highway Patrol as the investigating agency, and says it learned of the crash from police and the media.

Then it blacks out the crash narrative, the software version, and whether the road was within the system’s approved operating domain, all as “confidential business information.” That’s the same redaction Tesla applies to 99.9% of its reports.

The report also surfaced late. Tesla filed it as a 5-Day report, the urgent category for fatal crashes, but it didn’t land until Tesla’s September filings, more than three months after the crash. And Tesla lists law enforcement as one of the ways it found out about it.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 07:56 UTC, which converts to 3:56 a.m. in Florida, two minutes off the 3:54 a.m. in FHP’s report. The city, the highway, the 2023 model year, the month and the fatal outcome all line up, and it’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report in Naples that month. It’s the same crash.

A Tesla on driver-assist going highway speed into the underside of a big truck, in the dark, in Florida. If that sounds familiar, it should.

In 2016, Joshua Brown was killed near Williston when his Model S on Autopilot drove under a tractor-trailer crossing the highway. In 2019, Jeremy Banner died in Delray Beach when his Model 3 on Autopilot went under a trailer at 68 mph and had its roof sheared off. In both crashes, neither the driver nor the system braked.

Trooper Watson’s point was that a human couldn’t see the truck. But a big, unlit obstacle sitting across two lanes at night is exactly the kind of thing a driver-assist system is supposed to catch, and Tesla now sells FSD as nearly ready to drive with nobody watching. And an attentive driver could clearly see it, as the BMW driver did, and stop before the Tesla arrived.

We want to be fair about what the data doesn’t prove. “Engaged within 30 seconds” is the reporting trigger. Tesla’s 71 mph may be a telematics snapshot rather than the impact speed. And with the software version redacted, we can’t say whether this was Autopilot or FSD.

The NHTSA release that surfaced this crash, covering filings through October 15, also set a new monthly high. Tesla reported 264 driver-assist crashes in September 2026, beating July’s 236, which was itself a record. That’s up from 135 in March.

September may still grow as late reports come in. This Naples crash shows how late they can be.

Our merged dataset now holds 4,669 Tesla driver-assist crash reports since 2019, 69 of them flagged fatal. The same release added two other fatal reports, both “Verified Engaged” and both covered locally with no mention of driver-assist: a Model Y that hit a tree and burned in El Dorado Hills, California, killing three, and a Model X that hit a signal pole in Naples on September 30, killing a passenger. We’ll lay those out separately.

Three people died on I-75, including a man who got out of his car to help a stranger. Tesla knows its driver-assist was on, knows the speed, holds the telematics, and filed a federal report saying so. Then it sealed everything that would explain what the car did, and the public got a story about a dark truck.

That's what happens when the system has to identify all objects in the camera frame before it can start to estimate the objects position and then relative distance and then relative velocity. Unrecognizable objects will destroy all your logic. This is a design failure and not something Tesla can actually fix.

Compare that to radars and lidars that directly measure distances and relative velocities of everything in front of the car, regardless of what it is. That is a far better approach because you do not want the car the impact objects on its trajectory regardless of what those objects turn out to be.

Tesla’s whole pitch for FSD is that the car sees better than you do, and yet, Tesla vehicles on Autopilot and FSD keep crashing on stationary objects on the highway. It’s the same failure that killed Joshua Brown and Jeremy Banner years ago. If the system saw the truck and the driver overrode it, Tesla should say so. It was quick to do that in the Katy crash when the data helped it. If the system didn’t see it, that’s a safety defect regulators and owners need to know about.

Either way, the redaction protects Tesla, not the people on the road. It’s the same pattern we found in Vineland and in July’s four fatal crashes, and the crash count keeps setting records.

We’re asking the Florida Highway Patrol for the full crash report, whether its investigators got Tesla’s raw vehicle data, and whether they even knew the system was engaged. If they didn’t, the only party that knows what this car did is the one that sealed the file.

#4620. Plant-Based Milk Alternatives May Not Give You Enough Iodine. Here’s Why That Matters

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Replacing dairy with plant-based alternatives (PBAs), even partially, could substantially lower iodine intake, especially if those alternatives aren’t fortified, according to a recent study published in the Lancet Planetary Health.

The United Kingdom-based researchers found that only 12% of UK plant-based milk, yogurt, and cheese products analyzed were fortified with iodine. This compares with 61% for calcium and 46% for vitamin B12.

In the United States, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) provides guidance on the nutritional content of PBAs, but fortification with iodine is voluntary.

The study found that replacing as little as 20% of dairy intake with plant-based alternatives could increase the risk of inadequate iodine intake, particularly among adolescent girls and women of reproductive age.

“People often worry about a decline in calcium intake when they replace some of their dairy with plant-based alternatives. As a result, iodine is frequently overlooked. This study serves as a valuable reminder of iodine’s significance as a nutrient,” said Victoria Finn, MD, board certified endocrinologist at Medical Offices of Manhattan, who wasn’t involved in the study.

The study included analysis of UK plant-based milk, cheese, and yogurt products, as well as dietary data from 3,500 people.

The researchers used statistical modeling to predict how swapping dairy for PBAs might affect iodine and other nutrients.

The people who are most vulnerable to iodine inadequacy are adolescent females and people at reproductive age, especially those who are pregnant or who plan to become pregnant.

The researchers estimated that replacing 20% to 35% of dairy intake with PBAs would increase the proportion of people with inadequate iodine intake:

When the researchers modeled the replacement of all dairy products with PBAs, the proportion of adolescent females with inadequate iodine intake rose to 80%. Among females ages 19 to 49, that proportion remained relatively stable as replacement rates increased.

It is important to keep in mind that the study used dietary modeling rather than direct measurement of iodine status.

Iodine is important for thyroid hormone production, metabolism, and both fetal and child brain development.

“Your thyroid gland requires iodine to produce thyroid hormones, which play a crucial role in regulating metabolism and supporting normal growth and development,” said Finn.

She added that if you consistently consume too little iodine over an extended period, the thyroid gland may enlarge and eventually struggle to produce enough hormones. This condition is known as hypothyroidism, which can lead to various symptoms such as lethargy, sleepiness, weight gain, dry skin, and more.

“Hypothyroidism can be particularly dangerous during pregnancy, as the baby’s brain, nervous system, and organs rely heavily on the mother’s thyroid hormone during the early stages of development,” Finn added.

In the United Kingdom, dairy is a major iodine source due to cattle feed supplementation, not because dairy is naturally high in iodine.

In the United States, dairy is also an important source of iodine for the same reasons.

However, the risk profile for iodine deficiency in the U.S. may differ from the U.K., as iodized salt is also a significant source of iodine and is widely available in the U.S., but not in the U.K.

According to the National Institutes of Health (NIH), the recommended daily intake of iodine depends on your age.

Plant-based or plant-forward diets have grown in popularity, in part due to the health benefits they offer. For example, consuming less meat can reduce your risk of heart disease, type 2 diabetes, obesity, and high cholesterol.

However, as this study suggests, it may be possible to reduce your iodine intake when transitioning to a plant-based diet. There are ways you can protect your iodine intake when choosing a more plant-forward diet, though.

Check the labels on plant-based dairy alternatives to find those fortified with iodine. You can also read the nutrition label. Iodine may be listed as potassium iodide or potassium iodate.

Seafood, eggs, and iodized salt are all good sources of iodine.

You can also discuss iodine supplements with your healthcare professional.

“Iodine supplements should be taken with caution, especially without checking your thyroid levels,” said Finn. “Additionally, be cautious with kelp supplements, as their iodine content can vary, and excessive iodine intake can disrupt thyroid function.”

#4616. Infant Bleeding Cases Surge as More Parents Refuse Vitamin K Shots for Newborns

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

Two large studies published on November 5 link declining newborn vitamin K shot rates to a sharp increase in infant bleeding cases, including potentially fatal brain hemorrhages.

A research letter, published in JAMA Pediatrics, analyzed data on approximately 11 million infants from 2017 to 2025 and found that vitamin K administration declined from 97.7% to 95%, while cases of vitamin K deficiency bleeding (VKDB) nearly quadrupled.

A second study published in JAMA, based on data from 5.2 million U.S. infants, found that refusal rates more than doubled, rising from 3.1% in 2017 to 6.8% in 2025. Infants who did not receive the shot had a 47% higher risk of bleeding and more than twice the risk of intracranial bleeding.

Additionally, new data from Truveta suggest the trend is continuing: refusals of vitamin K shots increased by 57% between January and June 2026, rising from 5.2% to 8.1% of newborns.

Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting, and newborns naturally have very low levels. Without the preventive injection, infants are at risk for VKDB, which can cause sudden bleeding in the brain, gastrointestinal tract, and other organs. Late-onset VKDB can occur up to six months after birth, often without warning signs, and may be fatal.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) continue to recommend an intramuscular vitamin K injection for all newborns, ideally within 6 hours of birth.

The shot is not a vaccine; it is a nutrient injection that helps prevent dangerous bleeding. A single dose reduces the risk of late-onset VKDB by approximately 98%.

Experts not involved in the studies attribute the rise in refusals partly to broader vaccine hesitancy and mixed public health messaging.

“The decision to vaccinate a newborn or allow a vitamin K injection at birth is complex, with multiple factors playing a role in the ultimate decision,” said Graham Tse, MD, a pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA.

Some of these factors, Tse said, include conflicting messages from federal health agencies such as the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), both overseen by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., an outspoken critic of the childhood immunization schedule.

The vitamin K shot is not a vaccine, yet RFK Jr. has declined to reassure parents about its safety, despite the CDC’s current recommendation to administer it at birth.

Additionally, growing medical distrust among parents has led to refusal of routine newborn care, such as the vitamin K shot, Reuters reports.

Healthline spoke with Tse to learn more about the risks of refusing the vitamin K shot and what new or expectant parents should know about this routine newborn treatment.

This interview has been lightly edited and condensed for clarity and length.

Tse: The decision to vaccinate a newborn or allow a vitamin K injection at birth is complex, with multiple factors playing a role in the ultimate decision.

A contributing factor to the decline in vitamin K injection at birth, as well as in newborn hepatitis B vaccination, is the conflicting messages from the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC).

Recommendations from these entities and others are conflicting or do not align with established, research-based, and proven recommendations from organizations such as the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) and the Infectious Diseases Society of America.

When there are conflicting recommendations, it creates confusion and doubt among parents about what the best or right choice is for their child.

As well, there is so much misinformation on the internet, among influencers, and on social media that it is difficult to know what information is accurate, well-researched, and proven, versus what may be just someone’s opinion or belief.

Some are mistaking the vitamin K injection at birth for a vaccination, which it is not. Ultimately, all these factors are contributing to parents declining or delaying vitamin K injections at birth.

Tse: Declining the newborn vitamin K injection puts the newborn at significant risk of serious and life threatening complications from vitamin K-deficient bleeding (VKDB). This was previously referred to as hemorrhagic disease of the newborn.

VKDB can be as mild as bruising of the skin but can be as serious as bleeding into the brain, and newborns and infants can die from VKDB.

Declining vitamin K injection at birth is significant because of the serious and potentially life threatening consequences of deficiency of Vitamin K and not being able to clot the blood.

The vitamin K injection at birth is highly effective at preventing VKDB.

Tse: If a neonate or infant has vitamin K deficiency, the ability to clot their blood and stop bleeding is highly reduced.

All newborns are at risk of low vitamin K due to low body stores, low vitamin K content of breast milk, reduced ability of the gut to mobilize vitamin K, and poor transfer of vitamin K across the placenta.

When the blood cannot clot, bleeding from minor or minimal trauma can occur, and even bleeding without injury or trauma may occur. This can include bruises, bleeding from the mouth or gastrointestinal tract, bleeding from cuts or circumcision.

Bleeding can occur anywhere in the body, including in the brain, which can be catastrophic.

VKDB can occur from birth and through several months of life. Bleeding in the brain from VKDB, one of the most serious consequences, can occur at any time from birth to up to 6 months or so and can occur unexpectedly and suddenly. Vitamin K given at birth can prevent this risk of bleeding.

Tse: Vitamin K is a necessary vitamin that all humans need. Vitamin K is not a vaccination.

Newborns need vitamin K to prevent serious, significant, and often catastrophic bleeding during their first several months of life.

Vitamin K has been given to newborns in the United States for close to 70 years, is safe, is studied, and is proven to help prevent vitamin K-deficient bleeding.

I urge new parents to allow their newborns to receive the vitamin K injection at birth — it protects them, keeps them healthy, is proven safe, and is recommended.

#4613. ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’ Launches, Pre-Sales Reportedly Top $1.6 Billion

Our car experts choose every product we feature. We may earn money from the links on this page.

PlayStation players reportedly lead Xbox users by 3:1 in getting orders in for the hotly anticipated game.

If your domicile happens to exist, say, under a large boulder, you might not have heard that Grand Theft Auto VI is finally arriving at the stroke of midnight on November 19. Those of us who watch television, browse the web, scroll social media, listen to the radio, read the newspaper, flip through magazines, or consume outside info in any way are well aware of the video game, however. It’s the latest installment of the immensely popular “Grand Theft Auto” series, which combines a (surprisingly deep) vein of car culture with an immersive open world full of theft, fighting, drugs, and other violent delights.

While the previous games came out on a semi-regular schedule of one every few years, it’s been 13 trips ‘round the sun since the last one hit stores. (GTA VI’s development has been so delayed, it even inspired a meme.) Suffice it to say, there’s a lot of pent-up anticipation—even enough to spark half-founded panic headlines about millions of people around the world call in sick to play. But there’s another report that puts a bit more solid of a figure on the excitement around the game. According to digital analysis firm SensorTower, GTA VI has already racked up $1.65 billion in pre-sales ahead of its launch.

That correlates to a little over 17 million orders for the game so far, according to the report, with 75 percent of pre-sales going for the PlayStation 5 version and the other 25 percent for Xbox Series X|S consoles. The chart shows a fairly typical exponential curve growth over the last five months since pre-sales kicked off: a long period of incremental gains, followed by rapid acceleration in the last few weeks.

And GTA VI-based revenue seems likely to keep coming in to creator Rockstar Games’s coffers at quite a clip, considering initial reviews for the game have been stellar so far. While it may not be your typical automotive-themed driving game, the latest release seems all but sure to guarantee Grand Theft Auto remains a serious part of car culture for some time to come.

#4612. Tesla on Autopilot/FSD was going 74 mph before fiery crash that killed 3

A Tesla Model Y left a parkway in El Dorado Hills, California, hit a tree and burst into flames in September, killing three of the four people inside. Tesla’s own report to federal regulators says Autopilot or “Full Self-Driving” was engaged, with the car doing 74 mph.

The crash was widely covered in the Sacramento area as a fiery single-car wreck. None of that coverage mentioned a driver-assist system. It’s the latest case in our ongoing investigation into fatal crashes hidden in Tesla’s NHTSA data.

Late on Saturday, September 12, 2026, a 2024 Tesla Model Y with four people inside was heading west on Serrano Parkway, between Terracina Drive and Silva Valley Parkway. That’s a residential part of the Serrano community in El Dorado Hills, east of Sacramento.

According to the CHP’s Placerville office, the Model Y left the road “for unknown reasons,” hit a tree on the north side of the parkway, and caught fire. Officers got the call around 10:38 p.m. By the time they arrived, the car was fully engulfed in flames.

Charles Anthony Cameron, 30, of Sacramento, was thrown from the car and died at the scene. Alejandra Mendoza, 28, of Sacramento, and Kailauna Viola Mills, 28, of Roseville, were found dead inside once firefighters put out the fire. One of the two women was driving; CHP hasn’t publicly said which.

Mills lived in Arizona and was visiting family. Her uncle told CBS Sacramento she worked in the medical field and was supposed to get married next April.

A fourth person, a 28-year-old Sacramento woman, survived with major injuries.

CHP says the cause is still under investigation. Speed, impairment, and how the car left the road haven’t been released. And nobody has said a word about Autopilot.

Under NHTSA’s Standing General Order, automakers have to report crashes where a Level 2 driver-assist system was engaged within 30 seconds of impact and someone is killed or hurt. Tesla filed a report on this one.

It lists a 2024 Model Y, a consumer vehicle, and marks the “Engagement Status” as “Verified Engaged.” That’s Tesla confirming through its own telematics that Autopilot or FSD was on. It logs a pre-crash speed of 74 mph, a fatality, and the California Highway Patrol as the investigating agency.

Then it redacts the narrative, the software version, and whether the road was inside the system’s operating domain, all as “confidential business information,” the same treatment Tesla gives 99.9% of its reports.

The rest of the report is strangely thin. Tesla lists the roadway type as “Unknown” and what the car hit as “Unknown,” even though police said it was a tree. It checks only one source for how it learned of the crash: the media. So Tesla found out about a triple-fatal crash in one of its cars from the news, then went into its own data and confirmed its driver-assist was on.

How we matched it: Tesla logged the incident time as 05:36 UTC, which is 10:36 p.m. Pacific on September 12, within two minutes of the 10:38 p.m. call CHP responded to. The city, the 2024 Model Y, the month, and the fatal outcome all line up. It’s the only fatal Tesla driver-assist report from El Dorado Hills in the data. It’s the same crash.

Two of the three victims were found inside the car after the fire was out. The survivor got out of, or was pulled from, the wreckage, depending on the report.

CHP hasn’t said whether the doors played any role, and we’re not suggesting they did. But it’s a fair question to ask about any Tesla crash with a fire, now that NHTSA is writing new rules for emergency door releases after years of complaints about people getting trapped. We’ve asked.

This is the second triple-fatal crash in Tesla’s latest NHTSA filings where its driver-assist was verified engaged and the public never heard about it. The other one was on I-75 in Naples. Add Vineland and July’s four fatal crashes, and the pattern is hard to miss.

"what little effort went into the report"?

I disagree, a lot of effort went in to minimize the report, to portray it as an unremarkable accident.

That is the effort I find Tesla criminally responsible for.

The CHP need the full report, no redactions. If they chose to censor it that is their task, not Tesla's.

What stands out in this one is how little effort went into the report. Tesla knows the speed, knows the system was on, and has telematics. But it couldn’t fill in what the car hit, and it learned about three deaths in one of its cars from the news. Then it redacted the one field, the narrative, that would tell us what the car did.

Tesla wants regulators and customers to trust FSD with no one watching. That trust has to be earned with data. A company that seals the account of what its car did at 74 mph in a neighborhood, in a crash that killed three people, isn’t earning it.

We’re asking CHP Placerville whether its investigators knew the system was engaged, whether they got Tesla’s raw data or Tesla’s summary of it, and what they found about the fire and the doors. If CHP never got the full data, how will it ever determine the cause?

#4611. FDA Initiates Labeling Changes for GLP-1s Due to Rare But Serious Eye Disease Risk

Follow Healthline on our socials for all things health.

GLP-1 users have a new symptom to watch for: Sudden vision loss in one eye.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) announced on November 9 that it will require drugmakers to add information to the warning labels of Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, Zepbound and other GLP-1 medications about “a potential increased risk” of a rare eye condition called nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy (NAION).GLP-1 medications are approved to treat type 2 diabetes and to help people lose weight and keep it off.NAION joins a growing list of side effects linked to GLP-1s, adding a second eye warning to several labels.The U.S. labels for Ozempic, Rybelsus, Trulicity, Mounjaro, and Zepbound already warn about diabetic retinopathy, a diabetes-related eye disease, according to each drug’s prescribing information.The two conditions affect different parts of the eye. Diabetic retinopathy damages tiny blood vessels in the retina, the layer at the back of the eye that senses light, according to the National Eye Institute. NAION damages the optic nerve when it doesn’t get enough blood, according to the FDA’s announcement.Mihail Zilbermint, MD, director of endocrine hospitalists at Johns Hopkins, told Healthline he hasn’t seen NAION in his patients. He has seen vision worsen in some people after they start a GLP-1.“But we believe that’s probably related to rapid improvement in their sugar control, which can also be seen in someone who is starting insulin,” Zilbermint said.

A 2024 study published in JAMA Ophthalmology “initially triggered” the FDA’s review, the agency told Healthline.

The study found a higher risk of NAION in people prescribed semaglutide, the active ingredient in Ozempic and Wegovy, than in people prescribed other diabetes or weight-loss drugs.The authors wrote that more research is needed to determine whether semaglutide causes NAION.Joseph F. Rizzo III, MD, director of the Neuro-Ophthalmology Service at Mass Eye and Ear in Boston, served as the study’s corresponding author.

In a 2024 podcast, Rizzo said he and a resident saw three patients with NAION who were taking semaglutide for about a week.“And because NAION is a fairly uncommon disorder in the general population, the fact that we had three within a relatively short period of time led me to suspect that there was a higher risk of developing NAION in patients on semaglutide,” Rizzo said. The FDA analyzed clinical trials for multiple GLP-1 drugs and noted that NAION cases were reported with every GLP-1 on the market, according to its announcement. Those findings led the FDA to require the warning for the entire drug class, the agency told Healthline.

About 70% to 80% of people with NAION first notice vision loss when they wake up, according to StatPearls. The FDA listed these symptoms:

No treatment has been proven to reverse vision loss from NAION, according to StatPearls.

“Patients experiencing sudden, painless vision loss in one eye should contact their healthcare professional immediately and should not stop their medication without consulting their provider first,” the FDA told Healthline.

In the announcement, the agency told doctors to promptly refer patients with suspected NAION to an ophthalmologist.

The FDA listed these possible risk factors for NAION:

The FDA told Healthline that many people who take GLP-1s also have these conditions, which made reports of NAION in GLP-1 users “challenging” to interpret.

Across 126 clinical trials, the FDA found about 6 NAION cases per 100,000 people taking a GLP-1 for a year, and about 4 per 100,000 people taking a placebo or another diabetes drug for a year.In real-world data, NAION was more common with GLP-1s than with one type of diabetes pill, but the FDA found no significant increase compared with another type, the agency told Healthline.Zilbermint said patients who saw the news have worried about losing their vision. He tells them that “many of the serious harms, including the potential harm of NAION, are rare.”“The overall risk is still very small,” he said.

Regulators in other countries have added NAION warnings, mostly for semaglutide:

The FDA told Healthline the benefits of GLP-1s “continue to outweigh their risks when used as directed.”The FDA has also approved some GLP-1s to lower the risk of heart attack and stroke, reduce the risk of worsening kidney disease, and treat sleep apnea and a type of liver disease.Zilbermint said that “for most of my patients with obesity, diabetes and heart disease, the benefits clearly outweigh the risks.”“But we definitely have to decide patient by patient,” he added.

The labeling change applies to these medications, according to the FDA’s announcement:

As of publication, the FDA’s online label database did not yet show the new warning on the drugs’ labels.
